title: Year 10 Food Technology
exam_focus: Covers five units — Food Inequity, Food Trends, Food Safety & Hygiene (temperature danger zone, the 2-hour/4-hour rule, mise en place), Food for Specific Needs and Food for Special Occasions — with emphasis on definitions, legal figures and structured short answers.

questions.stem: What is the temperature range of the food safety 'danger zone'?
options: 0°C to 5°C
5°C to 60°C
-18°C to 4°C
questions.explanation_en: The danger zone for bacterial growth is 5°C–60°C, where harmful bacteria multiply the fastest, and temperatures below 0°C only slow down growth without killing the bacteria.
questions.source: Structured Responses (Sample Answers).pdf — The Danger Zone

questions.stem: Under the 2-hour / 4-hour rule, what must happen to potentially hazardous food that has been in the danger zone for more than 4 hours?
options: It can be returned to the fridge and used again the next day
It can be reheated to 100°C and then served
It must be thrown away because bacteria levels are too high
It can be frozen and kept for up to one week
questions.explanation_en: If food is left for over 4 hours, the bacterial count will be too high, and it must be discarded, as reheating or refrigeration won't fix the issue.
questions.source: Structured Responses (Sample Answers).pdf — The 2-Hour / 4-Hour Rule

questions.stem: A tray of cooked chicken has been sitting at room temperature for 3 hours. Under the 2-hour / 4-hour rule, which action is correct?
options: Throw the chicken away immediately
Eat it now, but do not return it to the fridge
Return it to the fridge and use it later
Reheat it, then freeze it for the following week
questions.explanation_en: Food left for over 2 hours but less than 4 hours can still be eaten, but it can't be put back in the fridge, as this will only chill the bacteria; only food that's been out for less than 2 hours can be refrigerated.
questions.source: Structured Responses (Sample Answers).pdf — The 2-Hour / 4-Hour Rule

questions.stem: To keep perishable food out of the danger zone, foods such as ham and salami should be stored at:
options: 4°C or below
8°C or below
About 22°C
About 60°C
questions.explanation_en: To slow down bacterial growth, food must be refrigerated at 4°C or below, as temperatures like 8°C or 22°C are too high to prevent bacterial multiplication.
questions.source: Structured Responses (Sample Answers).pdf — The Danger Zone（Industry Example）

questions.stem: In a commercial kitchen, 'mise en place' refers to:
options: Cleaning down kitchen benches at the end of service
Preparing ingredients and equipment before cooking
Plating the finished dish neatly for service
Ordering stock and checking supplier deliveries
questions.explanation_en: Mise en place refers to having all ingredients ready, including chopping onions, measuring seasonings, and preheating the oven, as skipping this step can lead to poor workflow.
questions.source: Term 1 · Assumed Knowledge Quiz 6: Mise en place；Structured Responses (Sample Answers).pdf — Poor Workflow

questions.stem: Which statement best defines food inequity?
options: Everyone in a country has equal access to safe, nutritious food
Some groups have limited access to affordable, safe food while others do not
Restaurants charge different prices for the same meal
People choose not to eat certain foods for religious reasons
questions.explanation_en: Food inequity highlights the issue of unequal access to sufficient, safe, and nutritious food, and should not be confused with religious dietary restrictions or personal choices.
questions.source: Term 1 · Food Inequity Assignment (Part 1 – Define)

questions.stem: According to the Term 1 unit, which group is identified as likely to experience food inequity in developed and developing countries?
options: Professional athletes on high incomes
People on low incomes or who are unemployed
Full-time university students living on campus
Food critics who review restaurants
questions.explanation_en: Low-income or unemployed individuals are typical examples of groups affected by food inequity, along with others like rural residents, women and children, the elderly, people with chronic illnesses, people with disabilities, Indigenous Australians, and the homeless.
questions.source: Term 1 · Food Inequity Assignment (Introduction — list of affected groups)

questions.stem: Which Australian organisation was listed in the Term 1 assignment as a charity that rescues surplus food and redistributes it to people experiencing food insecurity?
options: OzHarvest
Woolworths
MasterChef Australia
Fair Work Australia
questions.explanation_en: OzHarvest is a typical Australian food rescue charity that collects surplus food from businesses and distributes it to those in need, whereas Woolworths is a supermarket chain, and Fair Work is a workplace regulator, neither of which are charities.
questions.source: Term 1 · Food Inequity Assignment (Part 1 – charity list) (charity functions supplemented from syllabus knowledge)

questions.stem: The food trend known as 'snackification' refers to:
options: Replacing main meals with more frequent, smaller snacks
Eating only two large meals a day and no snacks in between
Removing all snacks from your daily diet
Selling snacks only through supermarkets
questions.explanation_en: Snackification refers to the trend of replacing traditional meals with more frequent, smaller, and convenient eating occasions, which is the opposite of reducing snacking.
questions.source: Term 2 · Food Trends: Quiz 4 Snackification and other Food Trends

questions.topic: Food trends · Ugly fruit and vegetables
questions.stem: Supermarkets selling 'ugly' fruit and vegetables is a trend that mainly aims to:
options: Charge a higher price for imperfect-looking produce
Reduce food waste by selling produce rejected as ugly
Replace fresh produce with canned produce
Encourage farmers to grow fewer vegetables
questions.explanation_en: This trend targets 'ugly' but perfectly edible produce to reduce food waste at the farm and retail levels, with the core selling point being waste reduction, not price increases.
questions.source: Term 2 · Food Trends: Quiz 3 Veggies and Fruit too ugly for the supermarkets

questions.stem: How do celebrity chefs most directly influence food trends?
options: By setting the official price of restaurant meals
By popularising ingredients and dishes through media exposure
By writing the national dietary guidelines used in all schools
By inspecting restaurants for food safety compliance
questions.explanation_en: Celebrity chefs popularise certain ingredients or cooking methods through TV shows, social media, and recipes, creating trends, but they don't set prices, dietary guidelines, or conduct health inspections.
questions.source: Term 2 · Food Trends: Quiz 2 Celebrity Chef

questions.stem: A person with coeliac disease must avoid:
options: All dairy products, such as milk
Gluten, found in wheat, barley and rye
All foods containing added sugar
All nuts, seeds and peanut products
questions.explanation_en: Coeliac disease is an autoimmune reaction to gluten, requiring a strict gluten-free diet for life, and is an immune response, not just a ordinary 'flour allergy'.
questions.source: Term 3 · Food for Specific Needs: Quiz 6 Coeliac Disease

questions.stem: A food with a low glycaemic index (GI) is best described as one that:
options: Raises blood glucose quickly and sharply
Is digested slowly and raises blood glucose gradually
Contains no carbohydrate or sugar at all
Must be avoided by everyone with diabetes at all times
questions.explanation_en: Low GI foods are digested and absorbed slowly, causing a gradual increase in blood sugar levels and a longer feeling of fullness, whereas high GI foods cause a rapid spike in blood sugar.
questions.source: Term 3 · Food for Specific Needs: Quiz 5 The Glycaemic Index

questions.topic: Special dietary needs · Allergy vs intolerance
questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a food allergy from a food intolerance?
options: An allergy involves the immune system, while an intolerance does not
An intolerance is always more dangerous than an allergy
An allergy can be removed by cooking the food thoroughly
They are two names for exactly the same reaction
questions.explanation_en: Food allergies are mediated by the immune system and can trigger severe reactions like breathing difficulties, whereas intolerances are often due to enzyme deficiencies and typically cause gastrointestinal discomfort.
questions.source: Term 3 · Food for Specific Needs: Quiz 8 Allergies and Intolerances

questions.stem: Which two nutrients are most important for reducing the risk of osteoporosis?
options: Iron and vitamin C
Calcium and vitamin D
Sodium and potassium
Protein and vitamin B12
questions.explanation_en: Calcium is the main mineral in bones, and vitamin D helps with its absorption; a lack of either increases the risk of osteoporosis, and taking only calcium without vitamin D reduces its absorption efficiency.
questions.source: Term 3 · Food for Specific Needs: Quiz 11 Osteoporosis

questions.stem: Iron-deficiency anaemia is best managed by including more of which foods in the diet?
options: Foods high in vitamin C only, such as citrus fruit and juice
Iron-rich foods such as red meat, legumes and leafy greens
Refined white flour products such as white bread
Foods high in calcium, such as milk and cheese
questions.explanation_en: The dietary focus for iron deficiency anaemia is on increasing iron intake, with red meat, beans, and dark leafy greens being common sources, and vitamin C can enhance iron absorption but is not a source of iron itself.
questions.source: Term 3 · Food for Specific Needs: Quiz 8A Anaemia

questions.stem: In Chinese New Year celebrations, long noodles are served because they symbolise:
options: Wealth in the form of gold coins
Longevity and a long life
The end of the harvest season
Good luck in school examinations
questions.explanation_en: Longevity noodles symbolise long life and are typically served uncut and unbroken, whereas gold ingot-shaped dumplings are associated with wealth, and the two should not be confused.
questions.source: Term 4 · Food for Special Occasions: Quiz 2 Chinese New Year

questions.topic: Special occasions · Day of the Dead
questions.stem: Día de los Muertos (Day of the Dead) is a celebration in which families:
options: Fast for three days to mourn deceased relatives at home
Build ofrendas with food to honour deceased relatives
Give children cakes with a hidden coin inside
Throw a decorated birthday cake into the sea
questions.explanation_en: The Day of the Dead is a Mexican celebration in early November where families build an ofrenda altar with the deceased's favourite foods and items, and its tone is one of remembrance and reunion rather than mourning or abstinence.
questions.source: Term 4 · Food for Special Occasions: Quiz 3 Día de los muertos

questions.stem: Discuss how poor workflow can impact a chef working in a commercial kitchen. In your answer, identify one cause of poor workflow and one way it could be improved.
questions.answer: Poor workflow is when a chef is unorganised in the commercial kitchen. It reduces the restaurant's efficiency in preparing food on time and lowers the quality of the food; it is caused by not completing mise en place or not following the recipe in a logical order, and it can be improved by preparing ingredients in advance and communicating clearly with the team.
questions.explanation_en: Structured short answers should follow the Is-Affects-Caused by-Improved by-Example format: define the concept, discuss its impact, causes, and improvement methods, and provide an industry example.
questions.source: Structured Responses (Sample Answers).pdf — Poor Workflow

criteria.t: Defines poor workflow as a chef being unorganised in the commercial kitchen
Explains the impact: it reduces the restaurant's efficiency in preparing food on time and lowers the quality of the food
Identifies one cause, such as not completing mise en place or not following the recipe in a logical order
Identifies one improvement, such as preparing ingredients in advance or communicating clearly with the team

questions.topic: Food equity · Inequity in developed countries
questions.stem: Food inequity also exists in developed countries such as Australia. Identify two groups affected and explain one factor that makes it hard for them to access nutritious food.
questions.answer: Groups affected include people on low incomes or unemployed, rural and isolated people, the elderly, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, people with disabilities and homeless people. One key factor is the cost of fresh food combined with limited transport, which makes affordable nutritious food physically and financially hard to reach.
questions.explanation_en: Answers should include 'two groups + one reason', and common reasons include price, transportation distance, accommodation conditions, or health restrictions.
questions.source: Term 1 · Food Inequity Assignment (Introduction and Part 1)

criteria.t: Identifies one group affected in Australia, such as people on low incomes, rural and isolated people, the elderly or homeless people
Identifies a second, different group affected, such as Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people or people with disabilities
Explains one factor, such as the cost of fresh food combined with limited transport making nutritious food physically and financially hard to reach

questions.topic: Food equity · Charities — role and limits
questions.stem: Explain how charities such as OzHarvest or Foodbank reduce food inequity, and outline one limitation of relying on charities to solve food insecurity.
questions.answer: Charities collect surplus or donated food and redistribute it, free or at low cost, to people who cannot afford enough nutritious food. A limitation is that supply is unpredictable and depends on donations, so they treat the symptom rather than fixing the underlying causes such as low income and high housing costs.
questions.explanation_en: To score points, explain how charities 'provide emergency relief' by collecting and redistributing surplus food, and then discuss how structural problems cannot be solved by donations alone.
questions.source: Term 1 · Food Inequity Assignment (Part 1 – charity research) + Part 4 (future strategies)

criteria.t: Explains that charities collect surplus or donated food and redistribute it
Explains that they provide it free or at low cost to people who cannot afford enough nutritious food
Outlines a limitation: supply is unpredictable and depends on donations
Explains that this treats the symptom rather than the underlying causes, such as low income and high housing costs

questions.stem: Explain how social media drives food trends such as the #foodie movement and snackification, and identify one risk this creates for consumers.
questions.answer: Social media spreads visually appealing food content quickly, so dishes and products become popular through shares, hashtags and influencer posts, and manufacturers respond with convenient snack-style products. One risk is that consumers may copy unhealthy or unverified food advice and choose foods for appearance rather than nutrition.
questions.explanation_en: Explain the 'mechanism of transmission' and 'risks' of social media, such as misleading nutrition information and portion control issues, and simply describing the phenomenon without explaining the mechanism may result in lost points.
questions.source: Term 2 · Food Trends: Quiz 6 #foodie；Quiz 4 Snackification and other Food Trends

criteria.t: Explains that social media spreads visually appealing food content quickly
Explains that dishes and products become popular through shares, hashtags and influencer posts, and manufacturers respond with convenient snack-style products
Identifies one risk: consumers may copy unhealthy or unverified food advice
Identifies a second risk: consumers may choose foods for appearance rather than nutrition

questions.topic: Special dietary needs · Energy needs of athletes
questions.stem: Explain why a professional NRL player has different daily energy and nutrient requirements from a sedentary office worker.
questions.answer: The NRL player trains and plays at high intensity for long periods, so he burns far more kilojoules and needs more carbohydrate to refuel muscles, plus extra protein for muscle repair and fluid and electrolytes to replace sweat losses. A sedentary office worker uses much less energy, so eating the same amount would lead to excess energy being stored as fat.
questions.explanation_en: Answers should focus on 'differences in energy expenditure leading to differences in carbohydrate, protein, and water requirements', and simply stating that athletes eat more is not enough to explain the distribution of nutrients.
questions.source: Term 3 · Food for Specific Needs: Quiz 4 Fuel Requirements for NRL Players；Quiz 7 Diet of an Olympic Athlete

criteria.t: Explains that the NRL player trains and plays at high intensity for long periods, so he burns far more kilojoules
Explains that he needs more carbohydrate to refuel his muscles
Explains that he needs extra protein for muscle repair, plus fluid and electrolytes to replace sweat losses
Explains the contrast: the sedentary office worker uses much less energy, so eating the same amount would lead to excess energy being stored as fat

questions.topic: Special occasions · Why we celebrate with food
questions.stem: Give two reasons why families and communities celebrate with particular foods, and support each reason with one example.
questions.answer: Food is used to mark significant events and bring people together, for example a birthday cake at a birthday party or a shared feast at Christmas. Particular foods also carry cultural or religious meaning and are used to pass on traditions, for example long noodles symbolising longevity at Chinese New Year.
questions.explanation_en: Provide two distinct reasons, one being 'social gatherings' and the other 'cultural or religious symbols', each with an example, and failing to explain the reasons and only providing examples may result in lost points.
questions.source: Term 4 · Food for Special Occasions: Quiz 6 Reasons for Celebrating with Food

criteria.t: Gives one reason: food marks significant events and brings people together
Supports it with one relevant example, such as a birthday cake at a birthday party or a shared feast at Christmas
Gives a second, different reason: particular foods carry cultural or religious meaning and are used to pass on traditions
Supports it with one relevant example, such as long noodles symbolising longevity at Chinese New Year

questions.stem: Explain why personal hygiene is the responsibility of every food handler. Give two examples of poor personal hygiene that could contaminate food.
questions.answer: Every food handler can pass bacteria or viruses from their body to food, and food poisoning outbreaks are often traced back to one person's hygiene practices, so each worker is legally and ethically responsible. Examples include not washing hands after using the toilet or handling raw meat, and coughing or sneezing over food or working while sick with gastro.
questions.explanation_en: The key points are that individual behaviour can contaminate entire batches of food and specific incorrect practices, such as not washing hands, working while sick, and coughing over food, which is covered in Food Handler Basics Module 2.
questions.source: Term 1 · Food Handler Basics Training (Module 2: Personal hygiene)

criteria.t: Explains that every food handler can pass bacteria or viruses from their body to food
Explains that outbreaks are often traced back to one person's hygiene practices, so each worker is legally and ethically responsible
Gives one example of poor hygiene, such as not washing hands after using the toilet or handling raw meat
Gives a second example, such as coughing or sneezing over food or working while sick with gastro
